title: Victim 'freaked out,' says witness
article: An employee at the hotel where Tamer Roha died while in police custody said he feared for his safety after seeing the agitated 27- year-old.
"He wasn't acting like a normal person," Pervez Ahmed told the court at the continuation of Roha's fatality inquiry in provincial court Monday.
"I was afraid he might hurt me. His behaviour was forceful, and I was afraid to go close to him."

Roha, 27, suddenly stopped breathing shortly after police handcuffed him at the Quality Inn on Banff Trail N.W. Roha was later declared dead at Foothills Hospital. His behaviour and how he was treated by police prior to his death on Sept. 4, 2002, are the focus of the inquiry, which adjourned last October.
Ahmed also described to the court how a sweat-drenched Roha, his eyes darting back and forth, had engaged in odd behaviour, such as repeatedly opening and closing a second door in the room.
"I saw the young man and he was screaming, 'The police are coming, the police are coming,' " said Ahmed. "I told him, 'Calm down, calm down.' But he did not -- he kept screaming."

Earlier, another former employee testified the room was in complete disarray, with furniture tipped over. "He seemed freaked out," said Aaron Dalton, adding Roha was unintelligible and appeared very upset.

Toxicology reports showed Roha had high levels of cocaine is his system. The cause of death was found to be cocaine-induced excitation delirium -- a profound agitation and the instability of the nervous system.
On Monday, Det. Robin Greenwood testified crime scene investigators had discovered cocaine in Roha's room and car shortly after he died.

Greenwood said drugs were found in a garbage can in the room, along with several rocks of crack cocaine in a plastic bag on the backseat of Roha's car. He also told the court Roha's family had admitted their son had experienced similar problems in the past and had been admitted to hospital.
Roha's family members, who are representing themselves at the inquiry, asked Greenwood if officers had used too much force in restraining their son.
"In my opinion, they did everything right," said Greenwood.
The inquiry continues today, with two doctors expected to testify about previous hospital encounters with Roha.
